product_from_film: Pax Historia is a map-based alternate-history game with AI-driven diplomacy and user-created scenarios.
explains_well: A Greenland negotiation example shows one choice leading to a rejection and wider international responses.
unclear: The film does not clearly show how the player submits an open-ended action or how a turn advances.
scenario: Explore alternate histories, negotiate over Greenland in a fictional game and create a custom scenario for others.
product_clear_basis: The Pax Historia identity at 18s is followed by diplomacy panels on an alternate-history map at 19s.

scenes.action: Colored maps accompany what-if questions about America/Greenland, Rome and the Soviet Union. A wider map combines several highlighted regions.
scenes.design: Dark geographic map, bright territory colors and captions.
scenes.purpose: Invite counterfactual play; these are fictional scenarios.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 0–10s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: An illustrated siege has Fortify, Resist and Observe buttons, followed by a fixed survival outcome. Pax Historia is then named on black.
scenes.design: Fantasy/historical illustration and three choice buttons.
scenes.purpose: Contrast the proposed game with fixed-path play.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 10–18s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: Roman Empire and neighboring territories appear with Diplomacy and World Events panels. Captions describe memory and adaptive responses, then a 35,000+ Daily card appears.
scenes.design: Map, dark text panels and large metric.
scenes.purpose: Introduce responsive agents and audience claim.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 18–31s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: The map shifts to the United States and Greenland. Captions offer negotiation, trade or invasion, then describe a negotiation rejected by Denmark, NATO involvement and EU sanctions. Diplomacy and event panels accompany the expanding map.
scenes.design: Map reframing, country labels and dark message panels.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 31–50s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: Create New Preset leads to custom map borders and forms for starting year, world background and simulation rules, then Play Now.
scenes.design: Scenario form and green action button.
scenes.purpose: Show user authorship of game worlds.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 50–59s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: A gallery lists popular and updated worlds. Creators Build, Players Pay and Creators earn Tokens overlay it.
scenes.design: Scenario thumbnail catalog and large white text.
scenes.purpose: Describe community scale and reward model.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 59–66s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

scenes.action: Pax Historia identity and paxhistoria.co hold on black.
scenes.design: White globe mark and long dark end card.
scenes.evidence: 1 fps source samples in 66–76.766s; state changes visible, exact transition timing/easing unverified.

sound.detail: Draft supports alternate-history questions, adaptive-agent claims, the Greenland game example and scenario publishing/reward model. Several names and opening words are garbled; captions clarify them. No delivery, music, effects or sync was verified.
sound.visual_relation: V01–V07; script explains fictional map events and creation controls.
sound.evidence: 381-speech.json draft plus captions; no validated listening.

categories.finding: What-if hooks → fixed-path contrast → responsive diplomacy → example consequences → scenario creation → community.
North America and a what-if caption lead into a Greenland question. The map immediately sets a geopolitical game context.
Strategy and alternate-history players are addressed; map diplomacy makes the game clear at 19s and creation tools at 50s.
Maps reframe between territories, panels appear and form text changes. Exact pan/zoom mechanics and transition timing are unverified.
Map views carry the main story; the siege-button comparison is a separate illustrative contrast before the product.
Dark blue maps use strong territory colors; black UI and white typography keep the presentation restrained.
Captions explain consequences more clearly than the small diplomacy paragraphs. Preset fields reveal authoring controls, while token economics remain a slogan.
ASR/captions support a narrated game explanation with recognition errors. Sound qualities remain unknown.
Music character and structure are unverified.
Effects and their sources are unverified.

categories.reason: No validated listening or paired audiovisual timing.

categories.finding: Map UI, illustrated siege, forms and scenario gallery are combined. Asset origin and live-game status are unverified.

categories.finding: Captions preserve the gameplay argument without checked sound; the player’s input and turn control remain missing.
Territory colors and labels establish focus, then diplomacy panels provide detail; small text competes with the broad map.
The 19s Greenland example is the clearest causal section. The final brand hold lasts roughly 11s.
The reshape-history promise receives a branching diplomatic example, but no player-entered action is clearly shown.
Counterfactual questions suggest curiosity and agency; audience response is unmeasured.
The Greenland example keeps one objective across negotiation and broader reactions, unlike the opening’s quick era changes.
Adaptive memory, unscripted behavior, player/world counts and token rewards are unverified claims. Map events are fictional gameplay, not real-world reporting or prediction.
Custom borders, dates and AI rules combine historical strategy with user-made worlds.
Show the input-to-turn step.
categories.experiment: Type one player proposal, submit it, show the turn advancing and highlight the resulting response on the same map.

categories.finding: For Tin, make a decision’s downstream effects visible.
categories.experiment: Change one campaign decision and trace the resulting schedule, asset and channel changes with consistent labels.

categories.finding: No human new-viewer test was performed.
categories.reason: The product summary is this model’s film-only reading.

lessons.keep: Use one diplomatic decision to demonstrate a chain of consequences.
try: Show a typed proposal, submission, turn advance and matching response.
For Tin, trace one changed decision into schedule, asset and channel changes.
lessons.avoid: Explaining agency only through narrated consequences without the player’s input.
lessons.open: Adaptive behavior, memory, game mechanics, reward model, scale claims and audio qualities remain unverified.
